processing: Made from single buds or one bud with a just-opening leaf, shaped into slightly flattened, straight leaves. Methods vary between the producers under this regional name.
harvest_season: Spring; the top grades are single buds or one bud with a barely opened leaf.
appearance_dry: Slightly flat, slender and even, tender green with visible down.
appearance_wet: Even, lively shoots in a bright tender green.
taste_profile: Fresh and brisk with a high, lasting aroma and a sweet return.

brewing.notes: These are ordinary settings for a bud-heavy green. A glass shows the shoots well; pour off fully between steeps.

vintage_note: Sold as the current spring harvest, usually by grade, with the earliest bud lots at the top. As with other greens it is for drinking fresh, ideally within a year. The name covers many producers, so the maker and harvest date tell you more than the name does.
description:
Hanzhong Xianhao is less a single recipe than a shared name for the fine green teas of the Hanzhong area in the Qinba mountains of southern Shaanxi. It is a protected geographical indication, and Xixiang county is its main producing area.

The standard material is tender: single buds, or a bud with a leaf just opening. The finished tea is slender, slightly flattened and downy. Because the name absorbed older local brands, details of the work differ between makers.

A good lot is fresh and brisk, with a high aroma and a clean sweet finish. It rewards cooler water and a light hand, as bud teas generally do.

Buy it by season and maker. Older names such as Wuzi Xianhao, Dingjun Mingmei and Ningqiang Queshe still appear on packets and point to narrower styles inside the same family.
history:
Hanzhong has a long record as a tea area and supplied tea to the old tea-horse trade. The name itself is young: from 2005 the city consolidated more than twenty local tea brands, first into three (Wuzi Xianhao, Dingjun Mingmei and Ningqiang Queshe) and then into one. Geographical indication protection was approved on 10 December 2007.

The unified name was promoted heavily from 2009, and in July 2020 it joined the second list of protected names under the China-EU geographical indications agreement.
